title: Arranging for the station and losing his staff job in 1946
summary: He arranged for Hank D'Amico's staff band, but felt he was hired as the token black musician in wartime; in 1946 he was dismissed with others and not rehired.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Working radio and television: network shows, studio staffs, talk-show bands

blocks.x: Then I had a lot of pupils. I was doing very good teaching and then I was working on the staff, too. Then finally Hank D'Amico and Vernon Brown and Billy Butterfield and a bunch of them came over on the staff and they all were playing with Paul Lavalle so I was playing with them. Then finally they gave Hank a band and I was the arranger. And I wrote a lot of things for that station while I was up there.

And then finally -- Hallwood said they hired me at that time because of the war, you know, and they wanted to make it look good that they had -- I was the only Negro in there, you know. They wanted to make it look good. So when the war was over, 1946 it was when I got my notice with 25 other men -- got their notice. And everybody was eventually hired back but me. And "Down Beat" had it in the paper, they said, well, with Barefield's seniority he should fight this. And I got a lot of calls to take up -- go back and fight the case.
